title: Deborah under the palm (Judges 4–5)
hookLine: a prophetess judges Israel and leads the army with Barak

lines: A PALM BETWEEN RAMA AND BETHEL.
cards: There's a palm tree in the hill country of Ephraim, between Rama and Bethel, and under it sits a woman. People come from all over Israel to bring her their quarrels: a field boundary, a stolen animal, a family feud.
She listens, and she decides. The tree is so tied to her that it's called by her name: Deborah, Debbora in the Douay-Rheims.

To the north, a king named Jabin has kept Israel under his thumb for twenty years with nine hundred chariots. Today we open the books of the judges and the kings, and the first person we meet under a tree is a woman.

teach.b: Judge here doesn't mean a robe and a gavel. In the Book of Judges the Hebrew word is shofet: someone God raises up to lead, to rescue, and to set things right. Deborah does all of it.
The Douay-Rheims introduces her this way: "Debbora a prophetess the wife of Lapidoth, who judged the people." A prophetess, so she speaks for God. A judge, so people come to her for justice.
Then the crisis. She sends for a commander named Barak, Barac in the Douay, and gives him God's order: take ten thousand men to Mount Tabor.

teach.h: IF THOU WILT COME WITH ME.
teach.b: Barak answers with a condition: "If thou wilt come with me, I will go: if thou wilt not come with me, I will not go." Deborah goes, but tells him the honor of the victory will fall to a woman.
And it does, in a way nobody expects: the enemy general, Sisera, flees on foot and dies in the tent of another woman, Jael.

Chapter five is a song, one of the oldest poems in the Bible by many scholars' reckoning, and it gives Deborah a title no general gets: "a mother arose in Israel." The Church reads this song with care.
Jael's deed is violent, and the text praises it in a time of war, so Catholic readers take it as Israel's history, not a model for living.
Deborah herself is remembered with honor: the leader who sat under a tree, heard her people, and went with them when they were afraid.

how: Catholics hear stories from Judges, among them Gideon's call, at weekday Mass in late summer of one year of the two-year cycle; Deborah's own chapters are not among those readings, so many meet her by reading the book itself.

o: a priest who offers sacrifices for the people
someone who rules on cases in a courtroom
a leader God raised up to rescue and do justice

games.q: under the palm — tap the pairs.
p: if thou wilt come with me, I will go
Hebrew: a judge who leads and rescues

s: in this book, a judge mainly runs a courtroom
a shofet is raised up to lead and rescue; Deborah also hears cases, but that's only part of it.
Barak refused to go to battle without Deborah
"if thou wilt not come with me, I will not go." she went.
Deborah's palm tree was called by her name

games.q: you're Deborah. you've given Barak God's order, and he says he won't go unless you come too. what do you do?
o: stay under the palm and send him alone.
go with him, and tell him the honor will fall to a woman.
games.why: she goes, and says the victory won't be credited to him. the general falls by the hand of another woman, Jael.

practice: Bring to mind a woman who has led you somewhere: a mother, a grandmother, a teacher, a boss, a nun, a coach, a neighbor who organized the whole street.
Remember a time she listened, decided, or went with you when you were afraid to go alone. If you pray, thank God for her by name.

wordCard.voice: Judge. In the Book of Judges, shofet: one God raises up to lead, rescue and do justice, like Deborah under her palm. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: judge, one who leads and sets things right. The book is Shoftim, Judges.

carryVoice: Your line: she judged israel. And that's week fifty-six: a donkey that speaks, the Shema, choose life, Moses on Nebo, Rahab, Joshua's house, and Deborah. Day three hundred ninety-two.
